affected_parts.quote: P. capsici can cause root, crown, and fruit rot in pepper, tomato, eggplant, and all cucurbits.

summary.value: Roots and stems near the soil line appear water-soaked, dark brown and soft, and whole plants or vines collapse quickly; in peppers distinctive black lesions form on rigid stems while foliage and fruit wilt and wither yet remain attached; infected fruit shows water-soaked areas that enlarge and become covered in gray to white sporangia. On eggplant symptoms also include large leaf spots, fruit rot, crown rot, and dieback of the growing tip.
summary.quote: Roots and stems near the soil line will appear water-soaked, dark brown in color, and will become soft. Whole plants or vines collapse quickly. In peppers, P. capsici causes distinctive black lesions to form on stems. Infected stems remain rigid but foliage and fruit wilt and wither, and remain attached to the plant.

diagnostic_features.value: In peppers, distinctive black lesions form on stems which remain rigid while foliage and fruit wilt, wither and remain attached; on fruit, sporangia-covered lesions have a yeast-like, gray to white appearance.

value: Manage water so that there is never standing water for longer than 24 hours anywhere in the field
Avoid planting susceptible crops in Phytophthora-infested soil and keep records of contaminated fields
Rotate with corn, small grains, brassicas, alliums, or other non-hosts (minimum 3-4 year rotation)
Plant in raised, dome-shaped beds (at least 9 inches for non-vining cucurbits and peppers) in well-drained areas of the field
Practice light irrigation or sub-surface drip irrigation to keep the soil surface dry; improve drainage, break up hardpan with a V-ripper, and avoid soil compaction
After working in infested soil wash soil from equipment, and always work in clean fields before infested fields
Mulch between rows with straw or leave cover crop stubble to reduce splash dispersal of inoculum
Biofumigation with brassica (especially mustard) cover crops
Practice good sanitation and do not discard cull fruit in the field
Avoid introducing the pathogen into a field and promptly destroy affected plants at the start of an outbreak to limit spread
Plant resistant varieties where available (e.g. hard-rinded pumpkins 'Lil' Ironsides', 'Apprentice', 'IronMan', 'Rockafellow', 'CannonBall'; bell peppers 'Conquest', 'Paladin', 'Emerald Isle')
Apply fungicides preventively starting before disease onset
Preventive fungicide programs: mefenoxam/mancozeb (Ridomil, Apron), copper compounds (Kocide, Basic Copper 53, Champ 2F), phosphorous acid fungicides (Prophyt, K-phite, Agri-fos)

Targeted preventive fungicides: in cucurbits Presidio, Ranman, Zing!, Gavel, Zampro, Revus, Curzate, Tanos; for pepper Omega 500 and Reason 500; Presidio, Revus, Forum and phosphorous acid fungicides labeled on eggplant
Soil-applied products: Orondis Gold (in-furrow/banded), Ridomil Gold SL (directed base spray), Regalia Biofungicide, Warhammer (chitosan)
Biofungicides/biologicals: Serenade, Double Nickel, Taegro, RootShield/Rootshield Plus, Actinovate, Mycostop, Stargus, Bexfond, BioTam (soil drench)
treatments.quote: the critical goal is to manage water so that there is never standing water for longer than 24 hours anywhere in the field

conflicts.note: PNW Handbook names the same P. capsici disease on eggplant 'Phytophthora Root Rot'; UMass notes Phytophthora blight causes a root, crown and fruit rot, so these are the same disease.
Cornell Long Island Vegetable Health refers to the disease as 'Phytophthora blight on eggplant'.
PNW describes P. capsici as 'a fungus-like microorganism'; functionally equivalent to oomycete.
Cornell source did not state the pathogen name explicitly (null); pathogen confirmed by UMass and PNW sources.
